results.result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about cortical arealization, stating that genetic mechanisms intrinsic to the neocortex control the patterning of primary sensory areas during early development, with Emx2 specifically determining V1 size and position. Higher order areas outnumber primary areas by roughly 10-fold, but mechanisms specifying them remain unexplored.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide well-established background information supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of cortical organization and arealization mechanisms, setting up the rationale for the study.

results.result: In ne-Emx2 mice with enlarged V1 (~150% of normal), the higher order cortical area complex (HO-5HT) between V1 and surrounding primary areas appears qualitatively larger. Multiple anatomical markers (5HT staining, DiI tracing, Rorb expression) consistently show anterior shifts in area borders and expansion of both V1 and adjacent HO regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C21 are well-supported by multiple complementary anatomical techniques (5HT immunostaining, DiI axon tracing, in situ hybridization) shown in Figures 1A-B and supplementary figures. The convergent evidence from different methodologies strengthens the conclusion that both V1 and HO are enlarged in ne-Emx2 brains.

results.result: Layer 5 projection patterns are altered in ne-Emx2 brains, with corticotectal projections extending more anteriorly and corticospinal projections extending less posteriorly. These changes are consistent with altered projection neuron identity and overall expansion of visual areas across multiple cortical layers, suggesting that primary and higher order area size changes are paralleled.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by DiI retrograde labeling data from layer 5 projection neurons (Figure 1C). The findings extend the area patterning changes beyond layer 4 to layer 5, demonstrating that the alterations affect multiple cortical layers. The interpretation is appropriately cautious and consistent with cited literature.

results.result: Functional intrinsic signal optical imaging reveals that V1 in ne-Emx2 mice has intact topographic organization with normal strength and axis organization, but expanded retinotopic maps (elevation: 138% ± 8.7%; azimuth: 143% ± 8.2% of wt). The 5HT-stained V1 area accurately corresponds to the functional V1 map, suggesting enlarged HO has not acquired ectopic V1-like properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are well-supported by functional imaging data (Figure 2A-B) with appropriate sample sizes (n=6 per genotype). The correlation between anatomical (5HT) and functional (intrinsic imaging) V1 boundaries validates the anatomical measurements and supports the interpretation that HO remains functionally distinct from V1 despite size changes.

results.result: Dual tracer experiments show that cortical neurons around the V1/HO border in ne-Emx2 brains maintain appropriate subcortical connectivity patterns (V1 to dLG, HO to PO) consistent with their intrinsic areal identity rather than their shifted topographic location. This demonstrates that increased V1 size is accompanied by concomitant enlargement and anterior shift of HO.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by dual retrograde tracer experiments (Figure 2C) with appropriate controls and sample sizes (wt: n=15, ne-Emx2: n=17). The finding that connectivity patterns follow areal identity rather than position is important for establishing that the enlarged areas maintain proper functional characteristics.

results.result: Quantitative analysis using whole-mount in situ hybridization (WMISH) with multiple molecular markers (Unc5d, Igfbp5, Cdh8, Lmo4) reveals that both V1 and HO are enlarged by approximately 145-148% in ne-Emx2 brains. The magnitude of genetic marker-defined V1 matches 5HT-stained measurements, validating WMISH as a reliable quantification method. The increase in HO is proportionate to the V1 size increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C43 are well-supported by quantitative WMISH data (Figure 3) with appropriate statistical analysis (p-values provided, n=4-11 per group). The use of multiple independent markers showing consistent results strengthens the conclusions. The comparison between WMISH and 5HT staining validates the quantification approach.

results.result: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC), marked by Lypd1 expression, shows a modest size increase (114.3 ± 5.2%) in ne-Emx2 brains that is not proportionate to the larger increases in V1 and higher order visual areas. This suggests that increased V1 size is specifically accompanied by proportionate size increases of related higher order visual areas, but not unrelated cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by Lypd1 WMISH data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistics (p=0.0225, n=4). The differential scaling of RSC versus visual HO is important for establishing specificity of the proportional scaling relationship. However, the sample size for RSC is smaller than for other measurements.

results.result: A novel conditional cortex-specific Emx2 knockout (cKO) mouse line shows the opposite phenotype to ne-Emx2: V1 is reduced to approximately 67-68% of wildtype size across multiple markers (5HT, Unc5d, Igfbp5, Cdh8, Lmo4), and HO is proportionally reduced (Cdh8-HO: 66.8 ± 2.9%; Lmo4-HO: 69.3 ± 2.4%). This demonstrates bidirectional control of both V1 and related HO size by Emx2.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C55 are well-supported by data from the newly generated cKO mouse line (Figures 4, 4—figure supplements 1-4). The generation and validation of the cKO line is appropriately documented. Quantitative measurements with multiple markers and appropriate statistics (n=5-10 per group) demonstrate consistent reductions in both V1 and HO that mirror the ne-Emx2 phenotype in the opposite direction.

results.result: Across an ~80% variation in V1 size (from cKO through wt to ne-Emx2), related HO size scales linearly with V1 size (Cdh8 regression: R²=0.99662; Lmo4 regression: R²=0.97555). This demonstrates that Emx2 activity during development controls linear matching of primary and higher order visual area proportions.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C63 are strongly supported by regression analysis (Figure 4C) showing excellent linear fits (R²>0.97) across three genotypes. The quantitative demonstration of linear scaling is a key finding. However, the regression is based on only three data points (genotypes), which limits statistical power despite high R² values.

results.result: The study demonstrates that genetic alteration of V1 size results in linearly scaled specification of both primary and related higher order cortical areas during development. Regardless of V1 size, related HO exhibit normal cytoarchitecture, genetic profiles, functional properties, and connectivity patterns. This indicates that Emx2 specifies a 'sensory cortical field' including both primary and higher order areas with defined borders, and that higher order area size is flexible rather than fixed.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62, C64, C66 synthesize findings from multiple experiments. The conclusions are well-supported by the combined anatomical, molecular, functional, and connectivity data presented throughout the manuscript. The interpretation that Emx2 specifies a unified sensory field is reasonable given the proportional scaling observed.

results.result: The manuscript proposes a sequential model where cortical intrinsic mechanisms specify generic primary and higher order visual cortex properties during early development, while geniculocortical input is needed later during postnatal development to terminally differentiate genetic distinctions between V1 and HO.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by citations to relevant literature (Chou et al., 2013; Vue et al., 2013). This represents an interpretation of the current findings in the context of prior work rather than a novel experimental result from this study.

results.result: The authors speculate that increased complexity of connections and micro-circuits among higher order cortical processing centers likely accounts for gains in cortical functions in gyrencephalic mammals with larger cortical surface areas, and that the linear scaling relationship has major implications for understanding neocortical development, organization, evolution, and variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are speculative interpretations about evolutionary implications and mechanisms in other species. While the speculation is reasonable given the findings, it extends beyond the experimental data presented. The manuscript appropriately uses cautious language ('likely accounts for', 'suggesting') to indicate these are hypotheses rather than demonstrated conclusions.

results.result: The manuscript describes methodological details including ethical approval, use of previously described ne-Emx2 mice, generation of a novel Emx2 floxed allele with loxP sites flanking exons 1-2, cortex-specific deletion using Emx1-IRES-Cre, and use of established intrinsic signal optical imaging methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 describe methods and are supported by appropriate documentation including Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for the targeting construct and citations to prior work. The generation of the cKO line is adequately documented with Southern blots, PCR, and validation of cortex-specific deletion.

results.result: The authors used 5HT staining to visualize primary sensory areas and defined a higher order cortical area complex (HO-5HT) in the caudal cortex outside V1, S1, and auditory areas. In ne-Emx2 brains, both V1 and HO-5HT appeared qualitatively larger than in wildtype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised major concerns about how HO borders were defined and whether the 5HT-negative region (HO-5HT) was consistently delineated across figures. They noted that 'VHO extends far beyond extrastriate visual cortex' and questioned the flattening technique's contribution to size measurements. In later rounds, reviewers requested renaming to 'HO-5HT' to distinguish it from the measured HO region, indicating the initial definition was problematic.

results.result: DiI labeling of thalamocortical axons from the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLG) revealed that TCAs terminate in a larger region in ne-Emx2 brains than in wildtype, with a sharp border indicating an anteriorly shifted V1/HO boundary.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed concern that 'labeling patterns are produced by injections at particular topographic locations' and requested that 'the experiment should indicate the LGN injection site and the projections in flatmounted cortex, superimposed onto 5HT labeled V1 in the same mouse.' This indicates uncertainty about whether the DiI labeling reliably demonstrates the claimed border shifts.

results.result: Area-specific gene expression patterns, particularly Rorb expression, showed sharp borders between areas that shifted anteriorly in ne-Emx2 brains, with the low-Rorb expression area (corresponding to HO) being larger than in wildtype.
results.evaluation: While reviewers requested additional 5HT staining of parallel sections to strengthen the analysis, they did not directly challenge the Rorb expression data or its interpretation. The gene expression patterns were used as supporting evidence throughout the review process without substantive critique of the findings themselves.

results.result: Layer 5 projection patterns showed that corticotectal projections extended more anteriorly and corticospinal projections extended less posteriorly in ne-Emx2 brains, consistent with altered projection neuron identity and expansion of visual areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about the layer 5 projection data. These findings were presented as supporting evidence for multi-layer areal patterning changes and were not challenged in the review process.

results.result: V1 and higher order area sizes are altered concomitantly in ne-Emx2 brains at the level of area-specific connectivity and gene expression across multiple cortical layers, suggesting that changes in primary area size are paralleled by similar changes in higher order area size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned whether the data support a causal relationship, noting that 'there was not enough evidence to conclude that V1 size controls the sizes of surrounding cortical areas' and suggesting instead that 'genetic factors intrinsic to cortex control the size of both V1 and HO areas in coordination.' This indicates the interpretation of concomitant changes was accepted but the mechanistic conclusion was uncertain.

results.result: Intrinsic signal optical imaging revealed that functional topographic organization was intact in ne-Emx2 mice, but retinotopic maps were expanded (elevation: 138% ± 8.7%; azimuth: 143% ± 8.2% of wildtype).
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested 'a more compelling demonstration' by marking reference points in the topographic map, staining the same flattened cortex for 5HT, and superimposing the images. They also suggested including 'information about the topographic representations in areas of the lateral extrastriate cortex,' indicating the functional mapping data needed better integration with anatomical markers.

results.result: The 5HT-stained V1 area accurately corresponds to the functional V1 map defined by intrinsic signal imaging, suggesting that enlarged HO in ne-Emx2 brains have not acquired ectopic V1-like functional properties.
results.evaluation: After revisions addressing reviewer concerns about correlating functional maps with anatomical markers, this correspondence between 5HT staining and functional V1 boundaries was accepted. Reviewers noted the revised data 'help to clarify the questions that were previously raised.'

results.result: Dual retrograde tracing experiments showed that cortical neurons around the V1/HO border maintain connectivity patterns consistent with their intrinsic areal identity (V1 to dLG; HO to PO) rather than their topographic location, even though these borders are anteriorly shifted in ne-Emx2 brains.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'the DiI and DiD injections into WT and ne-Emx2 mice are targeted to different topographic locations of V1 and areas within VHO' and that 'the cartoon of the mouse thalamus and the labels are inaccurate,' which 'weaken the conclusion that the corticothalamic projections are comparable.' This indicates uncertainty about whether the connectivity patterns truly reflect areal identity versus injection location.

results.result: V1-specific molecular markers (Unc5d and Igfbp5) showed enlarged expression domains in ne-Emx2 brains (~148% of wildtype), comparable to measurements from 5HT-stained sections (~142%), indicating that molecular markers reliably delineate V1 for quantification.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the molecular marker data for V1 delineation. The consistency between different measurement methods was accepted as validating the approach for quantifying area sizes.

results.result: Higher order visual area markers (Cdh8 and Lmo4) showed enlarged expression domains surrounding V1 in ne-Emx2 brains (Cdh8-HO: 145.7 ± 6.4%; Lmo4-HO: 144.9 ± 3.8%), proportionate to the V1 size increase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised persistent concerns about HO border definition, noting that 'the borders of VHO in WT and ne-Emx2 mice are different' and that 'Cad8 (WT) stained region around the tip and continuing along the medial border of V1 is much larger than indicated by the stippled line.' Even in the final round, reviewers requested revisions to 'the border of HO (wt/Cdh8) in Figure 3B,' indicating ongoing uncertainty about whether HO was consistently measured.

results.result: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) marker Lypd1 showed a modest size increase (114.3 ± 5.2%) in ne-Emx2 brains, not proportionate to V1 and higher order visual area increases, suggesting that V1 size increase is specifically accompanied by proportionate size increase of related higher order visual areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the RSC data or the interpretation that its non-proportionate increase supports specificity of the V1-HO scaling relationship. This finding was accepted as supporting evidence for the main conclusion.

results.result: Conditional cortex-specific Emx2 knockout mice (cKO) are viable with anatomically normal neocortex but show areal patterning changes opposite to ne-Emx2, including greatly reduced V1 size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the cKO mouse characterization or the observation of reduced V1 size. This was accepted as the complementary loss-of-function model to ne-Emx2.

results.result: Multiple molecular markers (Unc5d, Igfbp5, Cdh8, Lmo4) and 5HT staining consistently showed that V1 in cKO mice is reduced to approximately 67-69% of wildtype size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the V1 size measurements in cKO mice. The consistency across multiple markers was accepted as reliable quantification of the reduced V1.

results.result: Higher order area markers (Cdh8 and Lmo4) showed reduced expression domains in cKO brains (Cdh8-HO: 66.8 ± 2.9%; Lmo4-HO: 69.3 ± 2.4%), proportional to the V1 size reduction.
results.evaluation: Similar to concerns about HO measurements in ne-Emx2, reviewers noted that 'Cad8 (WT) and Lmo4 (WT) include weakly stained regions in medial extrastriate cortex, which are not included in cKO mice' and requested revisions to 'the medial borders of Cdh8 expression in wt and cKO.' This indicates uncertainty about consistent HO measurement across genotypes.

results.result: Across an ~80% variation in V1 size (from cKO through wildtype to ne-Emx2), related higher order area size changes linearly with V1 size (Cdh8 R²=0.997; Lmo4 R²=0.976), demonstrating that Emx2 activity controls linear scaling of primary and higher order visual areas.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the 'cleverly designed' experimental approach and did not challenge the linear relationship per se, they emphasized that the data do not support the conclusion that 'V1 size controls the size of surrounding higher order areas.' Instead, they suggested 'genetic factors intrinsic to cortex control the size of both V1 and HO areas in coordination,' indicating the mechanistic interpretation of the linear scaling remains uncertain.

results.result: Regardless of V1 size, related higher order areas exhibited normal properties (cytoarchitecture, gene expression, function, connectivity), demonstrating that Emx2 specifies a 'sensory cortical field' including both primary and higher order areas with defined borders, inconsistent with sequential or parallel specification mechanisms.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accepted that areas maintained their characteristic properties across genotypes, concerns about border definition and measurement consistency throughout the review process indicate uncertainty about the strength of evidence for the proposed unified 'sensory cortical field' model. The rejection of sequential/parallel mechanisms relies on the linear scaling interpretation, which reviewers questioned.

results.result: Higher order areas do not have fixed size but scale linearly with their related primary sensory areas, remaining proportionate when primary area size is altered through genetic mechanisms.
results.evaluation: After multiple rounds of revision addressing border definition concerns, reviewers accepted the core finding of proportional scaling. The final reviews indicated the paper 'has been improved' and 'seems ready for publication' with only minor abstract revisions needed, supporting acceptance of the linear scaling relationship itself.

results.result: Cortical intrinsic mechanisms specify generic primary and higher order visual cortex properties during early development, while geniculocortical input is needed postnatally to terminally differentiate genetic distinctions between V1 and HO.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this developmental model, which integrates the current findings with prior literature. The citations supporting the role of thalamic input in postnatal differentiation were accepted without critique.

results.result: The linear scaling relationship suggests that increased complexity of connections among higher order processing centers (rather than proportional area expansion) likely accounts for functional gains in gyrencephalic mammals, with major implications for understanding neocortical development, organization, and evolution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these broader speculative implications. While these claims extend beyond the direct experimental findings, they were accepted as reasonable interpretations of the significance of the linear scaling discovery.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C44-C46 regarding RSC data. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the finding that RSC shows non-proportionate scaling, validating the specificity of V1-HO relationship. OpenEval notes smaller sample size (n=4) as minor limitation; peer reviewers accepted this without challenge.

Perfect agreement on claims C67-C68 regarding evolutionary implications. Both evaluations support these speculative interpretations. OpenEval appropriately notes these extend beyond experimental data with cautious language; peer reviewers accepted the broader significance without challenge.

Significant disagreement on claims C39-C43 regarding HO quantification. OpenEval finds WMISH data well-supported with appropriate statistics; peer reviewers express persistent uncertainty about HO border definition, noting inconsistencies in border delineation across figures and genotypes, requiring multiple revision rounds.

Agreement on claims C36-C38 regarding V1 molecular marker validation. Both evaluations support the consistency between different measurement methods (WMISH vs 5HT staining). Peer reviewers accepted this validation approach without challenge.

Major disagreement on claims C11-C14 regarding HO enlargement. OpenEval finds anatomical evidence well-supported by multiple complementary techniques; peer reviewers express substantial uncertainty about HO border definition, flattening technique contributions, and consistency of the 5HT-negative region measurement, ultimately requesting renaming to 'HO-5HT'.

Disagreement on claims C15-C17 regarding DiI axon tracing. OpenEval finds the anatomical techniques provide convergent evidence; peer reviewers express uncertainty about whether labeling patterns reliably demonstrate border shifts, requesting superimposition of LGN injection sites with 5HT-labeled V1 in the same mouse.

Agreement on claims C20-C21 regarding Rorb expression. Both evaluations support the gene expression data. Peer reviewers requested additional 5HT staining for strengthening but did not challenge the findings themselves.

Agreement on claims C22-C24 regarding layer 5 projection data. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support these findings demonstrating multi-layer areal patterning changes. Peer reviewers did not raise specific concerns about this evidence.

Disagreement on interpretation of claims C25-C26 regarding concomitant changes. OpenEval supports the findings with appropriate caution; peer reviewers accept the observation but question the mechanistic interpretation, noting insufficient evidence for causal relationship and suggesting coordinated genetic control rather than V1 controlling HO size.

Disagreement on claims C27-C28 regarding functional imaging. OpenEval finds the intrinsic imaging data well-supported with appropriate sample sizes; peer reviewers express uncertainty, requesting better integration of topographic maps with anatomical markers through superimposition and reference points.

Agreement on claims C29-C30 regarding correlation between 5HT and functional boundaries. OpenEval supports the validation of anatomical measurements; peer reviewers initially uncertain but accepted after revisions addressing correlation concerns, noting revised data 'help to clarify the questions'.

Disagreement on claims C32-C34 regarding connectivity patterns. OpenEval finds dual retrograde tracer experiments well-supported with appropriate controls; peer reviewers express uncertainty about whether connectivity truly reflects areal identity versus injection location, noting inaccurate thalamic cartoons and different topographic targeting.

Agreement on claims C48-C50 regarding cKO characterization. Both evaluations support the generation and validation of the complementary loss-of-function model showing reduced V1 size. Peer reviewers accepted this without raising concerns.

Agreement on claims C51-C53 regarding V1 measurements in cKO. Both evaluations support the quantification showing reduced V1 with consistency across multiple markers. Peer reviewers accepted this as reliable measurement.

Disagreement on claims C54-C55 regarding HO measurements in cKO. OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate statistics; peer reviewers express uncertainty about consistent HO measurement, noting weakly stained regions included in WT but not cKO and requesting border revisions.

Disagreement on interpretation of claims C56-C57 regarding linear scaling. OpenEval supports the regression analysis showing excellent linear fits; peer reviewers acknowledge the 'cleverly designed' approach but question the mechanistic conclusion that V1 size controls HO, suggesting instead coordinated genetic control of both areas.

Partial agreement on claim C63 regarding proportional scaling. Both evaluations ultimately support the linear scaling relationship itself. OpenEval notes limitation of three data points; peer reviewers accepted the finding after multiple revision rounds addressing border definition concerns.

Disagreement on interpretation of claims C58-C62 regarding unified sensory field model. OpenEval finds the synthesis well-supported by combined data; peer reviewers question the mechanistic interpretation, emphasizing coordinated genetic control rather than V1-driven control of surrounding areas.

Disagreement on claims C59-C61 regarding rejection of sequential/parallel mechanisms. OpenEval supports the interpretation based on proportional scaling; peer reviewers express uncertainty about the unified 'sensory cortical field' model due to persistent concerns about border definition and measurement consistency throughout review.

Agreement on claims C62, C66 regarding core proportional scaling finding. Both evaluations ultimately support this after revisions. OpenEval finds conclusions well-supported; peer reviewers indicated paper 'seems ready for publication' after border definition issues were addressed.

Agreement on claim C64 regarding developmental model. Both evaluations support the integration with prior literature on thalamic input roles. Peer reviewers accepted the citations and developmental interpretation without critique.

Agreement on claim C65 regarding interpretation in context of prior work. Both evaluations support this synthesis with existing literature (Chou et al., 2013; Vue et al., 2013). Peer reviewers accepted without challenge.

OpenEval finds background claims C1-C8 well-supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as peer reviewers focused on experimental claims rather than background/introduction material.

OpenEval finds methodological claims C69-C73 regarding cKO line generation adequately documented with appropriate validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological documentation claims.
